title: Gluteal Tendinopathy and Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome
case: Case: A 54-year-old woman has 6 months of outer right hip pain that wakes her when lying on that side. She sits cross-legged and often stands with her weight on the right hip. Tenderness is over the right greater trochanter. Single-leg stance on the right causes pain at about 20 seconds. Hip range is full and painless, and the groin is not painful. No back or neurological findings, no red flags.

Working diagnosis: gluteal tendinopathy (GTPS). Plan: education on avoiding compression, isometrics, progressive hip abductor strengthening, graded walking, pillow between the knees at night, reassess every 3 to 4 weeks.
qa: Why avoid stretching the iliotibial band across the body? The stretch puts the hip into adduction and compresses the gluteal tendon against the bone, which may increase pain.
Why is the Ober test not used here? Its validity is limited, and it does not reliably identify the cause of lateral hip pain [Ref - to verify].
How do you separate GTPS from hip OA? GTPS has outer hip pain, trochanter tenderness and a full, painless hip range, while hip OA has groin pain and loss of internal rotation.
A runner has outer hip pain with impact and cannot hop. What do you suspect? A femoral neck stress fracture, so stop impact and refer for imaging urgently.
Why measure time to pain on single-leg stance? It is a simple, repeatable baseline that shows improvement in load tolerance.

fields.Purpose: Load the gluteal tendons in a compressive position to reproduce the familiar outer hip pain
fields.Position: Standing near a wall for safety, on the painful leg, with the other leg lifted
fields.Action: The patient stands on the painful leg for up to 30 seconds. Note the time at which pain starts and whether the pelvis drops
fields.Positive: Reproduction of the familiar outer hip pain, often reported within about 30 seconds [Ref - to verify exact criteria]
fields.Supports: A pain on single-leg stance with local tenderness supports gluteal tendinopathy
fields.Limits: Not specific; also positive with other hip and lumbar problems [Ref - to verify]
fields.Errors: Leaning the trunk toward the stance side to avoid load; allowing the lifted leg to touch the floor; stopping before 30 seconds without asking about pain
fields.Next step: Use the time to pain as a baseline for monitoring

fields.Position: Lying on the unaffected side with the painful hip slightly flexed, or supine
fields.Action: Press firmly on the greater trochanter and the lateral facet where the gluteus medius attaches
fields.Positive: Localised tenderness that reproduces the familiar pain
fields.Supports: GTPS; it is one of the most consistent findings
fields.Limits: Local tenderness alone does not separate tendinopathy from bursitis or other lateral hip pain

fields.Position: Supine with the hip and knee at 90 degrees
fields.Action: Passively rotate the hip outward, then ask the patient to rotate the leg back toward the middle against the therapist's resistance
fields.Supports: Gluteal tendinopathy, together with the other findings
fields.Limits: Accuracy has been reported to vary; use with other tests [Ref - to verify]

fields.Action: Stand on one leg for 30 seconds and watch the pelvis from behind
fields.Positive: The pelvis on the lifted side drops, or the trunk leans over the stance leg
fields.Meaning: Reduced hip abductor function; it is a sign of weakness or pain inhibition, not a diagnosis

redFlags.Finding: Pain with impact, a runner or someone with low bone density or low energy intake
redFlags.Immediate action: Stop impact; use crutches if painful on weight-bearing; refer for imaging

redFlags.Finding: After a fall: cannot bear weight, shortened leg, severe pain
Hot swollen hip or lateral thigh with fever
Constant night pain unrelated to position, weight loss, cancer history
Saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change
Sudden weakness with a gap or large pelvic drop after a pop

manual.name: Soft-tissue work to the gluteals, tensor fasciae latae and lumbar region
manual.application: Gentle sustained pressure; avoid heavy pressure directly on the greater trochanter

manual.name: Direct friction or stretching of the iliotibial band

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education, load management and exercise. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct. Do not use stretches that put the hip into adduction, such as the cross-body hip stretch, because they compress the tendon and may increase pain. Do not claim to release a tight iliotibial band.

exercise.Do instead: Sit with the knees apart and the feet flat

exercise.Avoid: Standing with the weight on one hip (hanging on the hip)
exercise.Do instead: Stand with the weight on both feet

exercise.Avoid: Sleeping on the painful side, or on the other side with the top leg dropping across
exercise.Do instead: Sleep on the other side with a pillow between the knees, or on the back

exercise.Avoid: Repeated stretching of the hip in adduction
Sudden increases in walking, hills, stairs or running

exercise.Exercise: Isometric hip abduction against a wall or band, lying on the back
exercise.Steps: Press the outer leg into a wall or band in a neutral position, avoiding crossing the midline
exercise.Starting dose: 5 holds of 30 to 45 seconds, once or twice a day [Ref - to verify]

exercise.Exercise: Side-lying hip abduction, bridge, sit-to-stand, mini-squat with a band
exercise.Steps: Slow control, keep the hip out of adduction
exercise.Progress when: Pain 3 to 4 out of 10 or less; easy

exercise.Steps: Control the pelvis, avoid hip drop
exercise.Progress when: Good control and no next-day flare

exerciseNotes: Principle: education to reduce tendon compression, together with a progressive hip abductor strengthening program, has been shown to give better outcomes than waiting and than a corticosteroid injection at longer follow-up in at least one large trial [Ref - to verify]. A short-term benefit from injection occurs in some patients, but it may not last [Ref - to verify].
Symptom rule: pain up to about 4 out of 10 that settles within 24 hours is acceptable [Ref - to verify]. Night pain and morning stiffness should not get worse. Increase load gradually.

Return to running (example): pain-free walking, good single-leg stance control, and tolerance of strength exercises at a moderate load. Start with short run-walk intervals and increase gradually. No fixed timeline is set.

modalities.name: Extracorporeal shockwave
modalities.indicated: Option for persistent pain after several months of care

modalityNotes: Medical options (decided by doctors): corticosteroid injection may reduce pain in the short term in some people, but repeated injections are not advised and long-term benefit is limited [Ref - to verify]. Other injections, and surgery for tears or persistent cases, are specialist decisions.
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.

Lateral hip pain with greater trochanter tenderness, pain lying on that side, pain on single-leg stance or other compressive loading, full hip range without groin pain? Yes: working diagnosis is gluteal tendinopathy (GTPS).
Groin pain, stiffness or reduced internal rotation? Yes: use the hip joint pathway.
Back or neurological signs? Use the lumbar pathway.
Begin education, load management and progressive strengthening.
If there is no improvement after a full trial, review the diagnosis and consider imaging and medical options.
Visit 1: screen flags and hip, lumbar and sacroiliac sources, explain GTPS as a load and compression problem, and teach positions to avoid.
Early: reduce compressive load, start isometrics, manage walking volume.
